**The Department of Unfinished Things**

There is a room on the seventh floor of the Municipal Records Building that does not officially exist. If you take the elevator from the lobby, the buttons go 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8. There is no 7. Press 8 and get out halfway, if you know how to listen for the pause between floors, and you will find a corridor that smells faintly of old paper and rain, even when it has not rained, because the windows at the end of the hall look out onto a courtyard that never gets sun. At the end of that corridor is a door with frosted glass, and in small brass letters it says, OFFICE OF DEFERRED COMPLETION. Underneath, in someone's ballpoint, added years ago and never removed, someone has written: *We do not finish. We witness.*

I have worked there for eleven years. My title, according to the city, is Senior Keeper, Grade III. My name is June. I have a desk, a stamp, a kettle that whistles too loudly, and a set of keys that open more doors than the building seems to have. My job is not complicated, and it is also impossible to explain at dinner parties, which is why I have learned to tell people I work in archives. That is not a lie. It is a simplification, the way a map is a simplification. A map leaves out most of the world so that you can find your way around the part that remains.

The building itself is unfinished, which feels appropriate. The east wing was planned in 1962, budgeted in 1974, begun in 1981, and abandoned in 1987 when the money ran out and the mayor who had promised it fell out of favor. The concrete stops mid-wall. Pigeons nest in the rebar. From the courtyard you can see the stairs going up to a floor that was never built, and sometimes in the winter the wind makes a low note through the hollow pipes, like a cello being tuned in another room. The Department of Unfinished Things was housed there because, as Mr. Patel in Personnel told me on my first day, "Who else would want it?" It was a joke, but it was also a kind of wisdom the city stumbles into now and then.

People find us. They almost never look surprised to be there. I used to think that was strange — a woman carrying a half-knitted sweater in a grocery bag, a man in a suit carrying a wooden boat hull under one arm as if it were a briefcase, a teenager with a friendship bracelet with one end longer than the other — but I have come to understand that most people know, long before they arrive, that they have been carrying something they started and did not stop, and did not finish, and cannot quite throw away. They bring it to us the way you bring a coat to a tailor, not expecting miracles, only care.

Our intake form is simple. One page. Object: ____. Started: ____. Stopped: ____. Reason for stopping, if you know it: ____. Reason for bringing it here: ____. Name and telephone number: ____. There is a line at the bottom that says, *Completion is not required. Continuation is not promised.* I make people read that line out loud, not because I am cruel, but because it changes the air in the room. Shoulders drop. Colleagues in other departments rush. We slow down.

Mrs. Alvarez came in on a Tuesday, which is our busiest day, because people seem to do their reckonings on Mondays and bring the evidence on Tuesdays. She was eighty-two, with hair in a tight silver bun and a purse that snapped shut with authority. She set a crossword puzzle on my desk, folded soft as cloth from being handled. It was dated, in pencil in the corner, 1979. "43 across," she said. "I have been thinking about 43 across for forty-six years. It is a seven-letter word. It means the thing you feel when you almost remember something." She smiled. "I still do not know it." I stamped it and put it on Shelf 12, which is for Mental Puzzles Abandoned Mid-Question, between a half-solved Rubik's Cube and a chess game where White has walked into a trap and Black has not noticed. Mrs. Alvarez wept a little when I gave her a receipt. "You are the first person," she said, "who has ever thought this was important enough to file."

The man with the boat hull was named Elias. He was fifty, and his hands were rough from rope and varnish. He had been building a sailboat in his garage for twenty years. Every spring he would sand it. Every autumn he would stop. "My son was supposed to help me launch it," he said. "He moved to Oregon. He has a baby now. He says we can launch it when the baby is old enough to help." He laughed, and it was not a bitter laugh. "That is a long time to wait for a boat." We put the hull in Bay 3, where the large things live: a piano with thirteen keys, a dressmaker's dummy with one arm missing, a bicycle with no chain. Elias visits it on the first Sunday of every month. He sits on a stool we keep for that purpose and talks to it, and sometimes he brings a sandwich and eats it in its company. He told me once that the boat does not feel abandoned. "It feels like it is resting," he said. "There is a difference."

Our shelves are organized not by type but by decade of abandonment. The 1950s are quiet and dusty and smell of tobacco. People from that era, when they left things, tended to leave them neatly, with instructions. The 1960s are louder; almost everything there hums. The 1970s are optimistic, full of things that were meant to change the world in small, practical ways — a solar-powered toaster, a novel about a lighthouse keeper who collects feelings, a community garden that was planted but never weeded. The 1980s are reflective and a little melancholy. The 1990s are earnest, full of half-written screenplays and businesses that were going to be different. The 2000s sprawl. Everything from the last twenty years asks to be digitally backed up, as if that would make it more finished, which it does not. The present decade is the smallest, because we are still pretending we will finish things this year.

We have rules, few and strict. We do not finish things. We do not start things. We do not judge things. We tag them, we store them, we check on them. Some require water. A small fern started as a houseplant and abandoned on a windowsill lives on my desk and is doing better than most houseplants. Some require music. A violin that was left mid-piece prefers the radio on low in the afternoon. Some seeds leak out of envelopes if you are not careful. Some things, if you put them next to other unfinished things, begin to talk to each other in ways I cannot describe without sounding fanciful, though I have worked here long enough to know that fanciful is not the same as false. A letter that needs an answer will, if placed near a question, sometimes grow a postscript all on its own. We do not encourage this. We simply note it in the log.

Every now and then, something finishes itself. This is the strangest part of the job, and the part I have never been able to write up in a report without Personnel sending it back with a note that says, "Please restate in administrative language." A quilt that was last touched in 1998 was found one morning complete, every square sewn, the backing turned and stitched. No one had signed it out. A couple who had left an unfinished argument in a sealed envelope in 2011 returned, asked for it back, read it together in the waiting area, and left holding hands, the envelope empty. A song that had been stuck on its second verse for a decade arrived back in the mail with the final verse added in a different handwriting. We do not claim credit. We simply file the finished things in a separate room, which we call, with great originality, the Finished Room. It is brighter in there. The air feels lighter. People who work near it tend to hum without knowing why.

In my bottom desk drawer, I keep my own unfinished thing. I have kept it there since before I worked here, since before I was qualified to keep anything. It is a letter. It begins, "Dear Dad," and then, on the next line, "I think I am writing this because..." and then it stops. I was eighteen when I started it. I was angry, and then I was hurt, and then I was embarrassed, and then I was grown, and every few years I would take it out and read it and add nothing. It lives in an envelope with a stamp from a post office that closed a long time ago. Some days I think I am keeping it unfinished out of respect for him. Some days I think I am keeping it unfinished out of cowardice. Most days I think the truth is in between, which is where most truths live, quietly, in the unfinished room of a person.

The rule, as you will have guessed, is that I cannot finish it here. I cannot bring my own things to my own desk and stamp them and put them on a shelf and call that honesty. So it stays in the drawer, and I check on it the way I check on everything else. Sometimes I hear it rustle. Once, I opened the drawer and found that a single word had been added underneath, in my own handwriting, but I have no memory of writing it. The word was "sorry." I do not know if it was there before. I do not know if I wrote it in my sleep. I left it. It felt important not to erase a word whose author I could not identify.

Last spring, on a Thursday when the rain had been falling sideways since dawn, a boy arrived with his mother. He was about nine, with a backpack too big for him and a notebook clutched to his chest like a shield. His mother did the talking at first. "His teacher," she said, "assigned free writing. She said, 'Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.' He has been staring at the page for three days. He cried last night. He said he doesn't know what he wants." The boy did not cry now. He looked at my desk, at the stamp, at the plant, at the shelves that went back beyond sight. "Are you a library?" he asked.

"Not exactly," I said.

"Do you have books that are finished?" he asked.

"We have many kinds of things," I said, "and we try to be kind to all of them."

He opened the notebook. The first page was blank except for his name in careful block letters at the top, NOAH, and underneath, in smaller letters, as if he were apologizing for the size of the assignment, 2500 WORDS. He had drawn a small line under it, as if to contain it. "What if I don't want to write about anything?" he said. "Is that allowed?"

His mother put a hand on his shoulder. "We told him people bring unfinished things here," she said. "He wanted to bring his."

I took the notebook, because that is what we do. We take things gently and we say, we will keep this safe. We stamped the intake form. Object: Notebook. Started: Three days ago. Stopped: Immediately. Reason for stopping: Did not know what he wanted. Reason for bringing it here: Teacher said write freely. I wrote nothing else. I put it on Shelf 1, which is for things that have not yet become what they are, and I gave Noah a receipt, which he folded very carefully and put in his pocket.

He lingered, though. Most people linger a little, even when they think they are ready to go. He looked at the boat hull in Bay 3. He looked at the fern. "Does it grow?" he asked.

"Slowly," I said.

"Does it mind?"

"I don't think minding is the right word," I said, "but I think it is glad to be here."

Noah nodded as if I had answered a question he had been saving up. "Can I come see it again?" he asked. "The notebook, I mean. Not the fern. Well, the fern too, if that's okay."

"Of course," I said. "It will be here."

That night, after the building emptied and the security guard made his rounds with his flashlight, I stayed late. The rain had stopped. The courtyard was glistening. I told myself I was doing inventory, which is true, and also not the whole truth, which is also true. I walked the shelves with my clipboard, as I always do, and when I came to Shelf 1, I stopped in front of Noah's notebook. It was a plain blue notebook, the kind that costs very little and lasts forever. I should not have opened it. Opening is not in the rules. But some rules are about not finishing, and some are about not interfering, and I have learned over eleven years that there is a third category, which is about care, and care sometimes looks very much like a small, rule-breaking act done quietly and without witness.

I opened it to the first page. Under NOAH and 2500 WORDS, someone — it could only have been me, though I do not remember deciding to do it — had written one sentence, in blue ink, in handwriting that was mine and also not quite mine: *This is about a boy who was asked to write freely, and he didn't know what he wanted, so he went to a room that keeps unfinished things, and he left his notebook there, and hoped it would learn how to want something on its own.*

I stared at it for a long time. I do not know if I wrote it that afternoon, or if I have been writing it, in pieces, for years without realizing. I closed the notebook. I put it back exactly where I had found it, at a slight angle, the way Noah had left it on my desk. I turned off the lights in the office. I locked the door. I walked down the corridor that should not be there, and pressed the elevator button for 8, and went down to the lobby, where the ordinary world resumed its ordinary business of people coming and going through revolving doors.

I have thought about that sentence often since. About how easily a single sentence can turn an ending into a beginning, or rather, turn a stopping into a resting. 2500 words is a strange number. It is too many to be a sentence and too few to be a life. It is a size that says, you have room, but not forever. Free writing, I have come to believe, is not about saying everything. It is about giving a thought enough room to find its own shape, without you standing over it with a ruler. Children know this instinctively. They draw a house with the sun in the corner, because the sun belongs in the corner when you are starting. Adults forget. We start in the middle and try to be impressive. We try to finish before we have begun.

Later that week, a man came in with an apology he had been carrying for thirty years. It was not on paper. It was in his posture, in the way he held his hands. "I said something to my brother," he said. "It was untrue, and I knew it was untrue, and I said it anyway because I was young and wanted to win." He did not want us to store it. He wanted to know if there was a way to un-say it. I told him, as gently as I could, that we do not have a department for that. We have a department for things that are paused. Un-saying is not pausing. It is something else. It is, perhaps, a different kind of work, done in a different room, with different tools. He nodded. "I will go and see him," he said. "He is in a home now. He may not know me. I will bring the apology with me anyway. I will say it into the air if I have to." I watched him go, and I thought about how many finished things are really just unfinished things that have learned to be carried differently.

People sometimes ask me, usually at the end of a visit, when they are putting on their coats, whether I think their thing will ever be finished. It is the question everyone wants to ask and no one wants to hear the answer to, because the answer is not yes or no. The answer is: it will become what it becomes, and that may look like finishing from some angles and like resting from others, and both may be true at the same time. A conversation that lasts a lifetime is not unfinished because it never concluded. A garden is not unfinished because you pull weeds forever. A walk along a coastline is not unfinished because you turn back before the map runs out. Some things are meant to end, and some are meant to be left open, like a door in summer, so that air can move through.

At five o'clock, I do my rounds. I check that the fern has been watered. I check that the violin is not too lonely. I check that the boat hull is level on its supports. I sign the log. I turn off the kettle. I lock the cabinet where the stamps live. The building makes its evening sounds — pipes, distant traffic, the pigeons settling on the unfinished wing. I think about the shelves, all those paused lives, all those almosts and not-yets and maybes, waiting not for someone to complete them, but for someone to witness them long enough that they feel less alone in their incompleteness.

Somewhere on Shelf 1, in a plain blue notebook, there is a boy's name and a number and one sentence that begins a story about a boy who did not know what he wanted. It is waiting for the second sentence. It does not know if Noah will come back to write it, or if someone else will, or if it will sit there for years, growing slowly like a fern, glad to be there. It does not need to know. That is the secret the Department of Unfinished Things keeps, stamped in blue ink on every receipt we issue: you do not have to finish to be kept. You do not have to know what you want to be allowed to want something. You can begin, and stop, and rest, and begin again, and all of those are honest ways to move through a life.

The elevator will take me down to 1, and I will walk home under whatever sky the city has provided that night, and in the morning I will come back, and the door will be there, and the shelves will be there, and the kettle will whistle too loudly, and someone new will arrive carrying something they started a long time ago, or three days ago, or just now, in the elevator, on the way up to a floor that does not officially exist. I will take it gently. I will stamp it. I will say, we will keep this safe. And somewhere, in the quiet, the unfinished thing will hear itself being named, and for the first time in a long time, it will feel like a beginning again.

Some things are meant to end, and some are meant to be left open, like a door in summer, so that air can move through.

At five o'clock, I do my rounds. I check that the fern has been watered. I check that the violin is not too lonely. I check that the boat hull is level on its supports. I sign the log. I turn off the kettle. I lock the cabinet where the stamps live. The building makes its evening sounds — pipes, distant traffic, the pigeons settling on the unfinished wing. I think about the shelves, all those paused lives, all those almosts and not-yets and maybes, waiting not for someone to complete them, but for someone to witness them long enough that they feel less alone in their incompleteness.

Somewhere on Shelf 1, in a plain blue notebook, there is a boy's name and a number and one sentence that begins a story about a boy who did not know what he wanted. It is waiting for the second sentence. It does not know if Noah will come back to write it, or if someone else will, or if it will sit there for years, growing slowly like a fern, glad to be there. It does not need to know. That is the secret the Department of Unfinished Things keeps, stamped in blue ink on every receipt we issue: you do not have to finish to be kept. You do not have to know what you want to be allowed to want something. You can begin, and stop, and rest, and begin again, and all of those are honest ways to move through a life.

The elevator will take me down to 1, and I will walk home under whatever sky the city has provided that night, and in the morning I will come back, and the door will be there, and the shelves will be there, and the kettle will whistle too loudly, and someone new will arrive carrying something they started a long time ago, or three days ago, or just now, in the elevator, on the way up to a floor that does not officially exist. I will take it gently. I will stamp it. I will say, we will keep this safe. And somewhere, in the quiet, the unfinished thing will hear itself being named, and for the first time in a long time, it will feel like a beginning again.
